philaster-or-love-lies-a-bleeding: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Philaster, or Love Lies a Bleeding, the title and list of persons, with no dialogue visible. The play is credited to Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher, and the scene is set in Sicily. The persons include the King, Philaster the heir to the crown, Pharamond, prince of Spain. Arethusa the king's daughter follows, and Eufrasia, a lord's daughter disguised as a page and called Bellario.
piano-and-song:
Friedrich Wieck's Piano and Song, translated from the German and published at Boston in 1875, tells how to teach, how to learn, and how to judge musical performances. The translator's preface introduces Wieck as a distinguished teacher who died in the autumn of 1873. He was father and teacher of Clara Wieck, the celebrated pianist who became Clara Schumann, and Robert Schumann himself had been his pupil.

His second daughter, Marie Wieck, was also a known performer. The translator believed Wieck's views would prove as valuable in America as in Germany. The little book preserves the method behind one of music's famous families.
piano-tuning: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of the Dover edition of J. Cree Fischer's Piano Tuning, the copyright pages and the start of its preface, with no instruction text visible. The Dover pages explain that this 1975 edition republishes the work first published at Philadelphia in 1907 by Theo. Presser, leaving out the dated chapters on the tuning profession and advertising. The title calls the book a simple and accurate method for amateurs.
podcast-joerogan-ELGY6HfkENg:
Author Michelle Dowd joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2137 to talk about her memoir of a hard childhood. Dowd grew up in a survivalist family in the mountains, under strict rules and deep poverty. Her book turned that hidden life into a public story.

She tells Rogan what daily life in that world was like, and how she found her way out through reading and school. Rogan asks about faith, fear, and the family she left behind. The episode is a quiet, gripping life story, and a look at the off-grid childhoods that exist far from public view.
podcast-joerogan-UlRHECIUNng: Bill Thompson with Rogan for episode 2473. The day's guest in a long, open talk. The full conversation as aired. A deep dive. One episode, dated, from the podcast shelves, kept for listeners and the curious.
podcast-tuckercarlson-BRgll1YUuNg:
A UFO whistleblower joins Tucker Carlson and says his life was in peril for speaking out. The episode title quotes his stark line on the risk. The guest is not named in the title, which fits the fear at the core of the talk.

The guest tells what he claims to know of the craft programs and what befell him when he spoke. He argues the state guards the secret with threats that cross into harm. Carlson asks why he speaks at all at such cost. Listeners get a tense first hand tale. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his account.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rH3QGv2L9ng:
A whistleblower joins Tucker Carlson to claim the state has run the largest spy program in all of history. The episode title also warns of a coming slave state. The guest is not named in the title, which adds to the sense of risk.

The guest lays out the scale of the watch net as he says he saw it from inside. He warns that the tools built for war abroad now turn on the home crowd. Carlson asks what can still be done to break the net. Listeners get a stark alarm in the guest's own words. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
pragmatism-a-new-name-for-some-old-ways-:
William James delivered the lectures printed here at the Lowell Institute in Boston in the winter of 1906 and at Columbia University in January 1907. Published them as Pragmatism, a new name for some old ways of thinking. He dedicates the book to the memory of John Stuart Mill. From whom he first learned the pragmatic openness of mind, and pictures Mill as the movement's leader had he lived. The preface confesses he does not like the name pragmatism, but it is too late to change it.

James unifies in broad strokes the tendencies suddenly precipitating out of the air in many countries: truth as what works in experience, beliefs judged by their fruits. He points beginners to Dewey and to F. C. S. Schiller's Studies in Humanism. Few philosophy books traveled further into ordinary speech.
principles-of-teaching:
Adam S. Bennion, superintendent of church schools, wrote a manual of teaching for class teachers in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The book first appeared in 1921 and was reprinted in 1952 by the general boards of the church's aid groups.

Early chapters ask what teaching is, why it is done, and what joy it brings, then turn to the teacher's own character and growth. Two chapters deal with personality and one with attainment. Church teachers get short, direct counsel on aims, preparation, and conduct in the classroom.
public-speaking:
Clarence Stratton, a director of English in a Cleveland high school, wrote a school text on speaking printed by Henry Holt with a copyright of 1920. The course treats a speech as a skill that can be broken into parts and practised.

Chapters cover speech itself, the voice, words and sentences, beginnings and endings, gathering material, planning, and making an outline or brief. Later chapters treat explaining, proving, refuting, debating, special occasions, and dramatics. Pupils get exercises and rules meant to turn shy speakers into clear ones, with appendixes and an index for class use.
queen-sheba-s-ring:
Queen Sheba's Ring is an adventure novel by H. Rider Haggard, told in twenty chapters by a narrator who begins by defending his friend Professor Ptolemy Higgs. Higgs had written of the tableland of Mur in North Central Africa. He had written of an ancient underground city in its ring of mountains. He had written of the strange tribe who live there. The tribe is of Abyssinian Jewish descent.

Higgs's rivals, the narrator says, have written him down as a man who strains the truth, and the tale that follows is the proof of his account. Chapter titles promise Sergeant Quick's advice, a death wind, an escape from Harmac, a den of lions, a burning palace, starvation, and a trial.
quit-your-worrying: Quit Your Worrying!, by George Wharton James, published at Pasadena, California, in 1916, is shown here by its dedication and contents. James calls to those standing on the banks of worry before the ocean of God's love to come on in, the water is fine. Twenty-three chapters name worry a curse of the age, then sort its kinds: health, parents, marital, religious, envy, ambition, jealousy, suspicion, impatience, and anticipation.
resonance-in-singing-and-speaking: Thomas Fillebrown, M.D., D.M.D., is named on the title page of this third edition of a book on resonance in singing and speaking. He served twenty-one years as professor of dentistry and oral surgery at Harvard, and lectured on voice development. Oliver Ditson issued the book, copyright 1911, in the Music Students Library. Fillebrown dedicates it to William Haskell Stockbridge, his instructor in voice culture. The opening pages shown are title and dedication only, so the book's chapters on the voice are not displayed here.
response-in-the-living-and-non-living:
Jagadis Chunder Bose, professor at Presidency College, Calcutta, published this study of response in living and non-living things with Longmans, Green in 1902. A line from the Rig Veda heads it: the real is one, though wise men call it variously. Bose dedicates the work to his countrymen.

A list of his earlier papers maps the research behind the book. He reported to a Paris physics congress in 1900 on how like the effects of electrical stimulus are in inorganic and living matter. Discourses at the Royal Institution and the Royal Society followed in 1901, with work on the electric response of plants under stimulus in 1902.
robert-browning:
Edward Dowden, professor of English literature in the University of Dublin, wrote this life of Robert Browning for the Temple Biographies in 1904. A portrait in oil, for which Browning sat to R. W. Curtis at Venice in 1880, fronts the book. The editor's preface, by Dugald Macfadyen, defines its task.

What readers want in Browning's case, the preface says, is a biography of the mind, in Gladstone's phrase. His life's events were achievements of the spirit more than public incidents. The book ties his poems to their dates and origins to show his inward growth. Browning's tonic optimism, it argues, clears the fog of materialism from life.
rough-and-tumble-engineering:
James H. Maggard wrote Rough and Tumble Engineering for men who run farm and traction engines, not for engineers of large fixed engines in fine engine rooms. In his preface he promises plain, everyday field terms and no science terms. His readers, he says, may do eight horse work one day and sixteen horse work the next. They may work one day with all in their favor and the next day in mud holes.

Maggard is frank that reading alone will not make an engineer of anyone. He asks for close reading, good judgment, and common sense. He claims that in one month a learner who follows the book can be, for real work, better than most so-called engineers. The opening pages address young men who wish to learn most of all.
rudyard-kipling:
John Palmer wrote Rudyard Kipling, first issued in New York in 1915 by Henry Holt and Company, with a front picture of Kipling. The contents list an opening survey, then chapters headed Simla, The Sahib, Native India, Soldiers Three, The Day's Work, The Finer Grain, and The Poems. Book lists for Britain and America and an index close the volume. Palmer's plan treats the Indian tales as a large bloc, then moves to later work and verse.

In the Simla chapter Palmer divides Kipling's Indian stories into three groups: tales of Simla, Anglo-Indian tales, and tales of native India. Kim, he adds, is more, much more, than a tale of India. He warns that the Indian stories tend to fill a share of space out of line with their weight. They count for less, he argues, than their number or the notice they have won would suggest.
schnitzler-casanova-s-homecoming:
An aging Casanova returns to Venice and finds himself a weary man haunted by his own legend. Arthur Schnitzler's novella Casanova's Homecoming, from 1918 and presented here in English, studies that return with melancholy precision. Desire has outlived desirability, and wit curdles toward bitterness in the old seducer.

Younger rivals, old flames, and the city's unchanged beauty all measure his decline. Schnitzler refuses both mockery and sentimentality, holding his hero in clear, cold light. The result ranks among the finest short works of twentieth-century European literature. Growing old has rarely been anatomized so gracefully. The novella shows a master of psychology working at novella length with perfect control.
school-and-home-cooking:
Carlotta C. Greer wrote School and Home Cooking while she led the foods and household management program at East Technical High School in Cleveland, Ohio. She shaped the book as a classroom text that pupils could follow step by step, both during lessons and later in their own homes. Its front pages picture the kitchen at Mount Vernon.

Greer begins with dishes and materials that beginners already know, then builds new skills on that ground. She puts off naming and sorting the food groups until pupils have worked with each one. Every section ends with related tasks covering table service, full meals, and projects to try at home. Those closing lessons also weigh meal cost, food value, wise choosing, and thrifty buying.
sermons-on-evil-speaking:
Isaac Barrow preached these sermons against loose and harmful talk, with an opening life of Barrow by Professor Henry Morley. Contents list pieces against foolish talking and jesting, against rash swearing, and two parts on the folly of slander. Barrow's own text treats evil speaking in general.

Morley traces Barrow from his London birth in 1630, through Charterhouse and Felstead schools, to Cambridge in 1643. Barrow won a Trinity fellowship in 1649 beside his friend John Ray, the plant scholar. The sermons apply that learning to daily speech, urging care with the tongue as a Christian duty.
sixteen-months-in-four-german-prisons-we:
Henry C. Mahoney told this tale of sixteen months in four German prisons, written down by Frederick A. Talbot for Sampson Low in London in 1917. The prisons named are Wesel, Sennelager, Klingelputz, and Ruhleben. A photograph shows Mahoney as he looked on his release day, taken by the German government itself.

A transcriber warns that gaps in the text stand as printed, cut by author, editor, or printer on purpose. Mahoney's account of arrest, hunger, and camp life in the Great War reached British readers while the war still raged, as first-hand proof of a civilian prisoner's lot.
sixty-years-of-california-song:
Margaret Blake-Alverson published this record of sixty years of California song at Oakland in 1913, from her own address on Second Avenue. A photograph by Webster of Oakland, dated 1912, shows the author. She dedicates the book to her friends everywhere, with a verse on singing through work and love.

Blake-Alverson states her terms plainly: if her singing and teaching bettered persons and communities, her work was well done. Pioneer concerts, teachers, and choirs fill her pages. The book preserves a woman musician's own account of how song grew with California from rough early days onward.
ski-running: Katharine Furse wrote Ski-Running, dated 1924, with a map and four photos. The opening pages give the contents alone. Heads cover the past of ski-ing, the cost of a ski-ing holiday, winter centres, clothing, and gear and its care. Later heads treat first steps, manners on the snow, snow and light, falls, tests, guides and teachers, maps and route finding, snow slips, mishaps, and the pull of the sport.
sport-and-work-on-the-nepaul-frontier-tw:
An indigo planter who signs himself Maori wrote Sport and Work on the Nepaul Frontier, dated 1878, as twelve years of sporting memories. A front picture shows tiger hunting and the return to camp. His preface says he went home in 1875 for a few months after some twelve years in India. There he met such deep ignorance of daily Indian life among folk at home that he saw room for a chatty, plain book.

His plan is to picture planter life in the mofussil, the country districts of India. He will tell of hunting, shooting, fishing, and other sports, and of work and play and plain daily events. He will also describe the natives as they show in close daily dealing: their ways, customs, bent, rites, and sayings, so far as these touch the planters' own social life. The book aims at friends at home, in a familiar and unshowy voice.
stage-confidences-talks-about-players-an:
Clara Morris, author of Life on the Stage and The Pasteboard Crown, writes Stage Confidences as talks about players and play acting. Charles H. Kelly printed the London book in 1902, with pictures, and Morris gives it to Mary Anderson. A front picture shows Morris herself in 1883. Her greeting speaks first to the dear girls who honor her with their liking and their confidences.

Morris grants the girls one edge over her: numbers. They can ask more questions in an hour than she can answer in a week, and fly into a hundred fits of vexed hope while she frames one soft answer. Their name is Legion, and their homes scatter between the two oceans. Some are grave, some gay, some well-off, some very poor, some wise. The greeting sets up a book of counsel drawn from a life on the stage, told as friend to friend.
stories-worth-rereading:
Stories Worth Rereading, dated 1913, is a set of short moral tales for young readers. No editor or author is named on the pages at hand; the contents alone carry the book, and they lean toward conduct, home, and faith.

Titles tell the drift: Their Word of Honor, What Rum Does, The Bridal Wine-Cup, My Mother's Ring, Honor Thy Father and Thy Mother, and Fighting the Good Fight. Other pieces praise song, a doctor's cow, and a boy's faithfulness to a dog, and the set closes with short lives of Samuel Smiles, the author of Self-Help, and David Livingstone. Temperance and duty are the steady themes.
studies-in-song:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Studies in Song was printed at London by Chatto and Windus in 1880. The contents begin with a Song for the Centenary of Walter Savage Landor, Swinburne's great elder and friend, and a grand chorus of birds drawn from Aristophanes.

The poems that follow include Off Shore and After Nine Years. They include a piece for a portrait of Felice Orsini. Evening on the Broads and The Emperor's Progress come next. The Fourteenth of July and The Launch of the Livadia follow. Six Years Old, A Parting Song, and the long By the North Sea close the book. Sea wind, public events, and private grief meet in verses built for sound as much as sense, hallmarks of Swinburne's art.
successful-methods-of-public-speaking:
Grenville Kleiser, once an instructor in public speaking at the Yale Divinity School, wrote Successful Methods of Public Speaking for Funk and Wagnalls of New York and London. Kleiser wrote a shelf of such manuals, from How to Speak in Public to Fifteen Thousand Useful Phrases, and this volume sums up his system.

The method treats speaking as a trainable power: building self-confidence in speech and manner, shaping ideas, using the voice, and holding an audience. Kleiser wrote for ministers, lawyers, salesmen, and club speakers in an age when platform skill could make a career. His books sold widely to self-improvers learning by mail and by practice at home.
swan-song:
Anton Chekhov's short play The Swan Song appears here in Marian Fell's English version, printed with her introduction and a chronological list of his works. The play's Russian author is spelled both Checkov and Tchekoff on the opening pages.

Fell's introduction sets the scene. Russia's last nineteenth-century years were grey with doubt and gloom. Its peasants were enslaved by want and toil. Its educated class was enslaved by idleness and tedium. Its idealists hoped for happiness two or three hundred years ahead. Chekhov, born at the Black Sea port of Taganrog on January 17, 1860, made that world his subject. The Swan Song itself is a one-act piece for an old actor alone in a dark theatre after the audience has gone.
talks-on-talking: Grenville Kleiser, once a teacher of public speaking at Yale Divinity School, wrote Talks on Talking, held under rights in 1916 by Funk and Wagnalls Company. Kleiser also wrote guides on how to speak in public and how to gain faith in one's own speech. Parts listed cover the art of talking, types of talkers, the speaking voice, how to tell a story, talking in sales work, and how to speak in public.
the-advancement-of-learning:
Francis Bacon wrote The Advancement of Learning, here copied from an 1893 Cassell and Company printing in London, Paris, and Melbourne. A front essay recalls the first title page of 1605, which named the work as two books on the growth of learning, divine and human, addressed to the king.

The essay hails it as a book still alive, one that opened a fresh world of thought. Bacon used it early in the reign of James the First to clear ground for his New Organon, his new tool of knowledge. Against it stood Aristotle's Organon, long drilled into students as the core of logic. Readers get Bacon's famed map of all learning, its gaps, and its blocks.
the-art-of-money-getting:
P. T. Barnum lays out golden rules for making money in this lecture. In the United States, he begins, land outnumbers people, so a healthy person willing to take any decent work that offers can find well-paid employment. Roads to success stand uncrowded on every side.

Yet Barnum grants that keeping money is the hardest thing in the world. The road to wealth, he quotes Dr. Franklin as saying, is as plain as the road to the mill: spend less than you earn. He invokes Dickens's Mr. Micawber as a comic witness to that simple rule, and builds his counsel on thrift joined to steady, chosen work.
the-art-of-public-speaking: Title pages alone present The Art of Public Speaking by J. Berg Esenwein and Dale Carnagey, copyrighted in 1915 by the Home Correspondence School of Springfield, Massachusetts. Esenwein is billed as author of How to Attract and Hold an Audience and works on the short story and the photoplay. Carnagey is named as a professor of public speaking at Baltimore. He also taught in Y.M.C.A. schools across several cities.
the-art-of-soul-winning:
J. W. Mahood wrote this handbook for personal workers. He was an evangelist and author of The Missing Wheel Found. Jennings and Pye printed it at Cincinnati in 1901. Eaton and Mains printed it at New York. A line from the Gospels heads it: he brought him to Jesus. Mahood's preface sees a crying need for a mighty revival in all the churches.

The key to such a revival, Mahood argues, is earnest personal work, and most church members are not ready for it. Many know nothing of a personal Pentecost; many are simply careless of their duty. He urges pastors to place a copy in every home a month before set revival meetings, with daily study, memory verses, and thought on the texts.
the-boy-allies-in-the-trenches-or-midst-:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies in the Trenches, or Midst Shot and Shell along the Aisne, dated 1915. The first chapter is called With the Army. It opens as two lads walk in on Field Marshal Sir John French, chief of the British force sent to help France. French is stunned to see them alive.

Lieutenant Paine and Lieutenant Crawford tell him they are not so easy to kill. They have been in Russia, they say, where they rode with a Cossack unit and saw much hard fighting. They came back by airship. Hal gives French a dispatch from Grand Duke Nicholas, chief of all the Russian hosts in the east. French, once the tale is told, puts both lads on his own staff at once. Rooms are to be made ready for them on the spot.
the-brain-and-the-voice-in-speech-and-so: F. W. Mott wrote The Brain and the Voice in Speech and Song, dated London, July 1910. Mott's name bears the marks F.R.S., M.D., and F.R.C.P. The list of heads starts with views on how speech began. The voice's three traits, loudness, pitch, and timbre, come next, then its three parts: the bellows, the reed in the larynx, and the resonator. The brain's work in speech and song, speech and right-handedness, and the seat of speech in the brain close the heads shown.
the-complete-works-of-robert-burns-conta:
Robert Burns's complete works, holding his poems, songs, and correspondence, appear here in an edition from Phillips, Sampson, and Company of Boston and J. C. Derby of New York, dated 1855. The title page promises a new life of the poet, with critical and biographical notices, by Allan Cunningham. The book is described there as elegantly illustrated.

A transcriber's note warns that hyphenation and accent vary through the book and have been left unchanged. The placing of poems, epitaphs, and songs also follows the printed original, indent for indent. A dedication to Archibald Hastie, Esq., member of Parliament for Paisley, begins after the title page, though its text is cut off in what is present. Cunningham's life was a standard doorway into Burns for nineteenth-century readers, and this American edition carried the Scots poet's songs and letters to a wide market in that form.
the-cords-of-vanity-a-comedy-of-shirking:
James Branch Cabell calls The Cords of Vanity a comedy of shirking. This revised and expanded edition carries an introduction by Wilson Follett. Follett frames the new edition as both a rescue job and an act of fresh creation, since Cabell reworked the novel rather than merely reprinting it.

Follett jokes that Cabell calls him the only known purchaser of the first edition. He quotes the old reviews with relish. A Cleveland paper found the book slushy and disgusting. A New York paper called it sterile, malodorous, and dull. Ainslee's Magazine found it rambling and at times nauseating. Such dull verdicts, Follett argues, cannot touch a writer who never counted them among his rewards or his penalties.
the-crossing: Winston Churchill's The Crossing is shown here only through its contents, split into two books. Book I, The Borderland, runs from The Blue Wall through Charlestown, the Nollichucky Trace, Harrodstown, and Kaskaskia, ending with The Hair Buyer Trapped and The Campaign Ends. Book II, Flotsam and Jetsam, takes its hero to Danville, across the mountains again, and on to St. Louis, with chapters on a keel boat and a strange city. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-crown-of-thorns-a-token-for-the-sorr:
E. H. Chapin subtitled his book The Crown of Thorns a token for the sorrowing. In a preface dated May 1860 he explains that one discourse in it, The Mission of Little Children, was written soon after a dear son's death. It was printed as a pamphlet. That printing sold out faster than the demand, so the piece returns here with others of like cast, most born of the same loss.

The contents list sermons on the three tabernacles, the shadow of disappointment, the Christian view of sorrow, consolation in loneliness, and resignation. Chapin offers the volume with his sympathy, hoping it may teach a troubled soul to endure and hope, and help the grieving weave the thorns that wound them into a crown.
the-crucifixion-of-philip-strong:
The Rev. Charles M. Sheldon, author of In His Steps: What Would Jesus Do?, published The Crucifixion of Philip Strong with Street and Smith under an 1899 copyright. Chapter I finds the minister unable to decide what is best to do. The postman has brought two letters, and Philip sits in his study, hands clasped over his knee, staring out the window in hard thought.

He calls his wife Sarah up from below. She comes teasing: he only summons her in great distress. The last time she had to cut him loose after he shut the tassel of his dressing-gown under the lid of his writing desk. Philip smiles and answers that he is fast again, in a strait between two choices, and begins to read her the letters.
the-dance-by-an-antiquary-historic-illus:
An unnamed antiquary wrote The Dance, printed in London by John Bale, Sons and Danielsson in 1911 and dedicated to Dr. Eleanor Maxwell. The subtitle promises historic illustrations of dancing from 3300 B.C. to 1911 A.D. In the preface the author calls the work a sketch of the picture-record of the dance, not a full history of the subject.

At most, he says, it sums up the history of posture, since a whole dance cannot easily be shown in pictures. A thorough treatment would take years and volumes; two writers alone gave eight hundred dances in four volumes. The old art of writing dances down, as music is written, is lost, and tries at reviving it have failed. He hopes the book will still serve readers studying the costume, positions, and gear of the dance across many periods.
the-deacon-of-dobbinsville-a-story-based: John A. Morrison subtitled The Deacon of Dobbinsville a story based on actual happenings. A preface by Lawrence D. Pruitt, dated March 1966, explains that the tale was first printed forty-five or fifty years earlier. It contrasts professors of religion with people converted and filled with the Holy Spirit. Pruitt quotes Morrison's leave to reprint, dated October 26, 1965. He notes that the author died at Anderson, Indiana, on December 23, 1965, in his seventy-third year, before the reprint appeared. Only that preface and the heading of Chapter I are present here.
the-eve-of-the-revolution-a-chronicle-of:
Carl Becker's The Eve of the Revolution, a chronicle of the breach with England in the Chronicles of America set, was printed by Yale in 1918. In his preface Becker owns that deeds alone are not his aim. He wants the feel of past minds at work, and he chases it through long quotes and free retelling. The air of an age matters more to him than its bare chronicle.

Stamp taxes, tea, and troops fill the tale, but ideas lead. Becker wrote for the series' Abraham Lincoln edition. His light touch made him a model for later historians of the founding.
the-fifth-string:
John Philip Sousa, famed for marches, wrote The Fifth String as a short novel of music and love, paired here with his tale The Conspirators. A violinist named Diotti stands at the center.

Diotti comes to America after triumphs in the great halls of Europe. The agent Perkins books him for a short run of concerts and talks him up without shame. On the night before his New York debut, Diotti shines at a rich hostess's reception, praised by men and women alike. A young woman in white catches his eye. Love and art pull at the star as his fame grows.
the-first-book-of-farming: Charles L. Goodrich, a farmer and expert in the Bureau of Plant Industry, wrote The First Book of Farming, printed at Garden City in 1923 from a first edition of 1905. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. The contents open with the broad rules of plant culture, starting with plants and then roots, their uses and habits of growth. No chapter text is included in this portion.
the-flag-raising:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote The Flag-Raising as a tale of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, in five chapters that end with The State o' Maine. Aunts Miranda and Jane Sawyer stand at the start.

Miranda grumbles that she never planned to raise any child, and that Rebecca's mother has palmed off the wild young one on them. Jane hopes the girl has had time to mend her ways. Miranda fears she has had time to grow worse. As the day of Rebecca's coming dawns, the stern farmhouse braces for a child whose bright talk and quick heart will shake its stiff rules.
the-good-time-coming:
T. S. Arthur wrote The Good Time Coming. It is dated 1855 at Boston and Philadelphia. His preface says life is a mystery. All men fix their eyes on the future. They wait for a good time that never comes. Years begin in hope and end in disappointment. Men gain little wisdom from the sharp lessons at every turn.

Arthur says he too has waited long for that good time. But hope should not die. A good time is coming for each person who works and waits for it. It must be sought in the right direction. Chapter I opens on a bright evening. It shows the lovely home of Edward Markland. Love and peace seem to dwell there. The tale will test that calm home. It will test it against the waiting and wanting of the preface.
the-grizzly-king: James Oliver Curwood wrote The Grizzly King, a romance of the wild. Frank B. Hoffman made the pictures. It is dedicated to the author's boy. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a list of illustrations. The captions are drawn from the tale. They tell of Thor, a great grizzly who has met porcupine quills before. Thor bears down on a caribou herd. Hunters read tracks in the sand and cry that if they hustle they can get their grizzly. No chapter text is present.
the-house-of-the-wolfings-a-tale-of-the-: William Morris's 1888 House of the Wolfings: Goths versus Romans in prose romance. The fantasy novel's founding epic, noble and strange. The well at the world's end begins here. Morris's Goths defy Rome, fantasy's founding epic.
the-laws-of-war-affecting-commerce-and-s:
H. Byerley Thomson, a Cambridge barrister of the Inner Temple, enlarged his treatise for a new edition in 1854. His preface says the first edition success among merchants encouraged large additions. He kept the plan and the concise, popular style that readers had welcomed.

A new introduction treats the origin of the laws of war in general, and an index aids reference. Contents open with the immediate effects of war and with enemies and hostile property. Thomson aimed at a working guide for traders whose ships and goods faced capture, blockade, and seizure.
the-library-of-work-and-play-gardening-a: Ellen Eddy Shaw wrote her gardening and farming book for young people in 1911, dedicating it to the boys of her club and to girls just as good as boys. Only the title page and contents of part one are present here. A garden club, indoor experiments, and a workshop end of the garden open the list. Later chapters cover strawberries, drainage, cabbage troubles, potatoes, and a corn contest. The lessons and club story themselves do not appear here.
the-life-and-work-of-susan-b-anthony-vol:
Ida Husted Harper wrote the life and work of Susan B. Anthony while Anthony still lived, and volume one appeared in Indianapolis in 1899. Her preface calls a lifetime biography unusual. Friends wanted the woman suffrage reform placed in history from unpublished records and living memory while correction stayed possible.

Harper admits Anthony often gave a different reading of letters and scenes than papers alone suggested. The volume holds public addresses, Anthony own letters, and letters from her contemporaries across fifty years. A dedication honors woman, for whose freedom Anthony gave those fifty years.
the-mad-king: Burroughs' 1914 Mad King thrones Barney Custer in Ruritania. Doubles reign. The Tower library holds the full text. It maddened king. Crowns confused. Swords flashed. Romance ruled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-path-of-the-king: The Path of the King, John Buchan's historical episodes. The king's path. This book preserves that history. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
the-perfect-wagnerite-a-commentary-on-th: Bernard Shaw's 1898 guide to Wagner's Ring cycle, reading the great operas as a socialist fable about gold, power, and love. Brilliant, willful, and hugely fun, it opened Wagner to English readers who feared him. Music writing as intellectual fireworks, from a critic who loved a fight.
the-reporter-who-made-himself-king: Davis' Reporter Who Made Himself King (1898) crowns a journalist in the Solomons. Audacity reigns. The Tower library holds the full text. It reported king. Press ruled. Natives bowed. Tale amused. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-rose-and-the-ring: Thackeray's 1855 fairy tale for children, a mock-heroic romp about princes, princesses, and a fairy gift that makes its bearer irresistible. Written for his own daughters, it parodies pantomime conventions with constant jokes and absurd plot twists. Funny for children and slyly funnier for adults, it is Thackeray at play.
the-social-cancer-a-complete-english-ver: José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere — The Social Cancer — is the great novel of the Philippines, exposing Spanish colonial cruelty through the story of Crisóstomo Ibarra. Its publication in 1887 ignited the movement for Filipino freedom; Rizal himself was executed for his writings. A masterpiece of political fiction and a nation's founding book.
the-strength-of-the-strong: Jack London's 1914 story collection, including fables of prehistoric men and tales of the South Seas. The title story imagines the birth of tribal law among cavemen, while others show London's socialist sympathies. Rousing and thoughtful by turns, it is late London at full power.
the-tinker-s-wedding: J. M. Synge's 1907 comedy about a tinker couple whose wedding plans are wrecked by a greedy priest and their own wild ways. Earthy, funny, and full of the music of Irish speech, it celebrates those who live outside respectability. Synge's most high-spirited play.
the-wallet-of-kai-lung: More of Ernest Bramah's delightful Kai Lung stories: the Chinese storyteller spins wry, elegant tales within tales, each a gentle satire on human folly. Written in mock-classical English that parodies translation, they are unique in literature. Charming, wise, and very funny.
thomas-hart-benton-s-remarks-to-the-sena: Thomas Hart Benton's 1837 Senate speech demanding the formal erasure of the censure against President Andrew Jackson. The Missouri senator's long campaign to vindicate Jackson was a landmark of party loyalty and constitutional argument. This record preserves a famous moment when Congress literally rewrote its own history.
tieck-the-pictures-the-betrothing:
Two novellas by Ludwig Tieck share this English volume: The Pictures and The Betrothing. Art and illusion drive the first, a story of paintings and the lives they distort. Love and misunderstanding drive the second, where a betrothal tangles on pride and mistaken readings of hearts.

Both tales show the German Romantic at his most characteristic. The everyday and the uncanny keep trading places, and mystery hides inside ordinary drawing rooms. Tieck's irony stays gentle; his strangeness creeps rather than leaps. Elegant and quietly unsettling, the pair suits readers who like their Romanticism in a minor key. The volume makes a fine doorway into his shorter fiction.
un-un-res-united-nations-declaration-on-:
Human cloning is condemned in this United Nations declaration, adopted by the General Assembly in 2005. States had argued for years over a cloning treaty and split over research uses of cloned embryos. In the end they settled for a non-binding declaration that passed by a divided vote.

The text calls on states to ban all forms of human cloning that clash with human dignity. It also urges laws against genetic work that threatens human life. Supporters saw a moral stand. Critics said the wording swept too wide. The declaration records where the world argument stood in 2005.
united-states-dept-of-state-corresponden: Correspondence in relation to the killing of prisoners in New Orleans. The State Department file. This book preserves that correspondence. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
vanished-arizona-recollections-of-the-ar: Martha Summerhayes's memoir of army life in Arizona Territory in the 1870s, when she followed her officer husband to remote desert posts. Witty and observant, she describes heat, hardship, and frontier society with a New Englander's amused eye. A rare woman's view of the military frontier, and a delight to read.
walking: Henry David Thoreau's great essay in praise of walking and wildness, first delivered as a lecture. "In Wildness is the preservation of the World," he declares, urging readers to saunter through woods and fields as a spiritual practice. The founding text of American nature writing, as fresh and bracing as a walk itself.
washington-irving: Charles Dudley Warner's Washington Irving: the great storyteller's life. The biographer's affectionate portrait. An American classic.
